1:
When the blow fell, the witnesses watch a single man turn the whole city into a theatre of grief. The reformed John Gill asks first how Mordecai came to know of it — whether by report, by common fame, or by the sight of the edicts already posted in Shushan; the Jewish tradition, he notes, would have it revealed to him in a supernatural way, by Elijah in the one Targum, by the Holy Ghost in the other. However he learned it, he rent his clothes, put on sackcloth with ashes, went into the midst of the city, and cried with a loud and bitter cry. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole movement of the scene: Mordecai went mourning and lamenting through the city even to the king's gate, and Haman's decree drew a like lamentation from the Jews in every province of the empire.

The puritan Matthew Henry will not let the grief be read as mere passion. Mordecai not only vented his sorrow but proclaimed it, unashamed to own himself a friend to the Jews and a fellow-sufferer with them, their brother and companion in tribulation, however despicable and odious Haman's faction had made them appear. It was nobly done, Henry says, thus publicly to espouse what he knew to be a righteous cause, and the cause of God, even when it seemed a desperate and a sinking one. Mordecai laid the danger to heart more than any, for he knew Haman's spite was aimed first at himself, and that it was for his sake the rest were struck at; yet, able to appeal to God that he had acted from conscience, he could commit his own cause and his people's to him that judgeth righteously — for God will keep those who are exposed by the tenderness of their consciences. The wesleyan Adam Clarke adds the vivid word the Greek puts in his mouth as he cried through the streets: a people who have done no evil are going to be destroyed.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, hears something conspicuous in the very fullness of the mourning. The sorrow of Mordecai, and of the Jews in v.3, is described by outward signs alone — torn garments, sackcloth and ashes, fasting, weeping, wailing — with nothing said of prayer or of any crying to the God of Israel who is able to save. Daniel, Ezra, and Nehemiah were Jews who under alien rule besought their God and were heard, as in Daniel 6:10, Ezra 8:23, and Nehemiah 1:4; here that note is, strikingly, unsounded. The wesleyan John Wesley reads the loud cry more simply, as the expression of Mordecai's deep sense of the mischief coming upon his people, and calls it bravely done thus openly to espouse a just cause even when it seemed a desperate one.
2:
A law bars the mourner from the gate, and the witnesses read in it the whole vanity of a court that would banish sorrow by decree. The reformed John Gill notes the plain purpose of Mordecai's coming: he pressed as near as he might to the king's gate, that Esther, if it were possible, might be made acquainted with the calamity now hanging over her people. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the topography and the rule together: “even before the king's gate” means the open space before the entrance to the royal palace, for none might pass within it wearing mourning; the Hebrew, they observe, says flatly that there is no entering — none may enter so clad.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke agrees that Mordecai could not go in to the place where the officers waited, being in a mourner's habit, which the law forbade. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses beneath the rule to its motive: nothing sad or ill-omened must meet the monarch's gaze, as though, by shutting his eyes to the presence of sorrow, sickness, and death, he might the more successfully evade them.

The puritan Matthew Henry turns the statute into a satire on the pride of power. The arbitrary rule of these kings had set many a subject mourning, yet none in mourning dress might come near the king, who was not willing to be troubled with the complaints of such; nothing but the gay and pleasant might appear at court, for all in kings' palaces wear soft clothing, as in Matt. 11:8, and not sackcloth. But to keep out the badges of sorrow, unless they could also keep out its causes — to forbid sackcloth to enter, unless they could likewise forbid sickness, and trouble, and death to enter — was a mere jest. And so, Henry notes, the law obliged Mordecai to keep his distance, coming only before the gate and not taking his accustomed place within it. The wesleyan John Wesley lands on the same irony: the sackcloth was barred lest it give the king any occasion of grief; but what did that avail, to keep out the tokens of sorrow while its causes pressed in unhindered? The witnesses converge: a throne may forbid the sight of grief, but it cannot forbid the thing itself, and the barred gate only measures how far such a court has walled itself off from the misery it makes.
3:
The grief that filled the capital now fills the empire, and the witnesses follow the decree wherever it runs. The reformed John Gill marks its reach: in every province to which the king's commandment came, appointing the Jews to destruction on the set day, the same lamentation broke out among them, wherever they were to be found. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the wording — “in every place” standing as an adverbial phrase for wherever the decree arrived — and render the closing clause with care: sackcloth and ashes were spread for many, that is, many sat in hairy garments upon the earth where ashes had been strewn, the very posture of mourning described in Isa. 58:5. All the Jews, they conclude, broke out into mourning and weeping and wailing, while many showed their grief in that extreme and public form.

The puritan Matthew Henry dwells on how total the sorrow was. The Jews in every province laid the sentence much to heart, denying themselves the comfort of their tables — for they fasted, and mingled their tears with their meat and drink — and the comfort of their beds at night, for they lay in sackcloth and ashes. And Henry hears a note of self-reproach in it: those who, for want of confidence in God and affection to their own land, had stayed behind in the land of their captivity when Cyrus gave them liberty to be gone, now perhaps repented of their folly, and wished, when it was too late, that they had complied with the call of God to return home.

Here the wesleyan Adam Clarke registers the astonishment that will echo through the rest of the chapter: fasting, and weeping, and wailing — how strange, he exclaims, that in all this there is not the slightest intimation given of praying to God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott had noticed the same silence, that the grief of the Jews is set down in outward manifestations only, with no word of entreaty to him who is able to save. The witnesses do not here resolve the difficulty; they simply lay it open, and it is a real one. A whole people mourns, fasts, and wails from one end of the empire to the other, and the historian who so carefully records their sackcloth records not one prayer — a reticence the commentators will read very differently before the chapter is done, some hearing in the very fast an unspoken cry to heaven, others a strange and telling silence, but which none of them can here pass by unremarked.
4:
The tidings pass at last through the palace wall, and the witnesses watch the queen's grief answer the mourner's. The reformed John Gill supposes her maids and eunuchs told her the thing merely as a piece of startling news, or perhaps only that Mordecai was in sackcloth; and he infers from their bringing it that they had marked some peculiar respect between the queen and this man at the gate. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render her reaction strongly: on hearing it she was seized with convulsive grief, the Hebrew an intensive form for being wrung with pain; and she sent raiment to Mordecai to put on in place of his sackcloth, evidently that he might be able to enter the palace and give her the particulars of what had happened — but Mordecai would not accept it.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke reads her motive plainly: she supposed he must somehow have been stripped of his clothing, and therefore sent him more. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds it fair to infer from the whole exchange that Esther's connection with Mordecai was known to those about her, though as yet not to the king. The wesleyan John Wesley reads the gift of raiment to the same end as Keil and Delitzsch: she clothed him that he might be capable of returning to his former place, if not of coming in to her to acquaint her with the cause of his sorrow.

The puritan Matthew Henry gathers the pathos of it. Upon a general intimation of the trouble Mordecai was in, Esther was exceedingly grieved; his grief was hers, such a respect did she still retain for him, and the Jews' danger was her distress, for though a queen she forgot not her relation to them. Let not the greatest, Henry urges, think it below them to grieve for the affliction of Joseph, though they themselves be anointed with the chief ointments, as in Amos 6:6. She sent him change of raiment, the oil of joy for mourning and the garments of praise for the spirit of heaviness; but because he would make her sensible of the greatness of his grief, and so of the greatness of its cause, he received it not, but was as one that refused to be comforted. The refused robe becomes the first word of his appeal: he will not be soothed out of a sorrow he means her to feel.
5:
Since the mourner will not come in and the queen may not go out, a messenger must run between them, and the witnesses attend to the man she chooses. The reformed John Gill names him Hatach, one of the king's chamberlains appointed to wait on her; the Targum, he notes, would have this be Daniel, but it is not likely Daniel should have lived to this time. Whoever he was, the king had entrusted him with the care of the queen, and she in turn had so high an opinion of him that she employed him in this delicate affair. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe her errand exactly: she sent Hatach, one of the eunuchs the king had set to attend her, to learn of Mordecai what this was and why it was — the meaning and the cause of his going about in mourning.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke reads the appointment with a colder eye on the Persian court. This eunuch the king had set over her partly to serve her and partly to observe her conduct; for no despot, Clarke remarks, is ever exempt from that twofold torture, jealousy and suspicion. The attendant who carries the queen's secret is also, by his office, the king's watchful eye upon her.

The puritan Matthew Henry sets the scene within the iron confinement of the harem. So strictly did the laws of Persia shut up the king's wives that it was not possible for Mordecai to have any conference with Esther about this weighty affair; all their commerce must be carried by messengers, and Hatach was one she could confide in. She sent first to know more particularly and fully what the trouble was that Mordecai now lamented, and why he would not put off his sackcloth. To enquire thus after news, Henry adds, that we may the better know how to direct our griefs and our joys, our prayers and our praises, well becomes all that love Zion; if we must weep with those that weep, we must first know why they weep.

The witnesses leave the queen doing the one thing open to her — asking, and asking through a trusted go-between. It is a small but telling picture of her powerlessness: the woman raised above every subject of the empire cannot cross a courtyard to speak with the man who reared her, but must sift the meaning of his sackcloth through the report of a servant. Clarke's cold observation hangs over the whole exchange, that the very eunuch she trusts is also the king's appointed watcher; and Gill's caution about the Targum's Daniel reminds us how little even the tradition could settle about so obscure a figure. Yet upon this obscure man, going out and coming in across the open square, the whole weight of the following scene will rest, and so the long negotiation of the chapter begins in the mouth of an eunuch running between a barred gate and a curtained throne.
6:
The exchange must happen in the open, and the witnesses fix the place with some care. The reformed John Gill has Hatach go forth to Mordecai unto the street of the city, where he stood in the public view, openly expressing his grief and sorrow. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the word: what our version calls the “street” is rather the broad open place, the square before the gate, the Hebrew rehob. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch place it precisely — the open space of the city that lay before the king's gate — and it was there, in that public square, that Mordecai laid the whole matter before the messenger.

The setting is not idle. Because the law of v.2 forbade the man in sackcloth to pass the gate, and the custom of the court forbade the queen to come out, the whole of this grave business had to be transacted across a threshold that neither could cross — Mordecai barred by his mourning, Esther walled within the palace. The puritan Matthew Henry had made just this point: so strictly were the king's wives confined that no direct conference was possible, and every word must pass by the hand of Hatach going to and fro.

So the eunuch comes out to the mourner in the square, and the reader is made to feel the strangeness of it: a matter touching the life of a whole nation is entrusted to a servant carrying messages between a weeping man in the street and a queen behind her curtains. The witnesses do not divide over the verse; they simply mark the stage on which the rest of the scene is played. Every step of the deliverance that is to come must begin here, in the open place before the gate, where the one man who knows the danger stands where he cannot be admitted, and where the one woman who can avert it can be reached only through the mouth of another.

There is a further fitness in the setting that the commentators leave the reader to feel. The broad square before the palace was the very place of concourse and business, the point where the city met its king; and it is there, in full public view, that Mordecai has planted himself and his sackcloth, so that the eunuch must come to him under the eyes of all. Gill's note that he stood openly expressing his grief joins with Ellicott's rehob and Keil's open space to make one picture: the protest is not hidden in a private house but pressed upon the threshold of power itself. The bare notice that Hatach went out to Mordecai is, in the historian's hand, the setting of a conference on which everything now turns, held in the one place where the barred and the walled-in could at last, through a third, be brought to speak.
7:
Now the mourner tells his whole tale, and the witnesses note both its substance and its sting. The reformed John Gill unfolds what Mordecai reported of himself: how, for refusing to reverence Haman, he had drawn that man's fury upon himself, and upon all the Jews for his sake, so that Haman had vowed revenge and framed a whole scheme for their ruin. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the second thing Mordecai told — the exact sum of money that Haman had promised to weigh out into the king's treasuries for leave to destroy the Jews; the Hebrew word, they say, means a clearly stated amount, and it is brought forward here as the chief point of the report, the price at which a people's life had been bought.

The puritan Matthew Henry reads the message as an authentic and pointed account, sent with a charge attached. Mordecai told Hatach all that had happened to him — what a pique Haman had conceived against him, and by what arts he had procured the deadly edict — so that Esther might see the whole ground of the danger. And Henry passes on a tradition the Jewish writers, fruitful in invention, attach to this moment: that Mordecai, going home the night before in great heaviness at the news of Haman's plot, met three Jewish children coming from school and asked each what he had learned that day. The first said his lesson was, be not afraid of sudden fear, from Prov. 3:25; the second, take counsel together, and it shall come to nought, from Isa. 8:10; the third, I have made, and I will bear, even I will carry and will deliver you, from Isa. 46:4. “O the goodness of God,” Mordecai is made to cry, “who out of the mouth of babes and sucklings ordains strength!” The story is legend, and Henry offers it as such; but it catches the truth the verse itself carries, that a man crushed by a decree of death is nonetheless reaching, even in his grief, for a hope beyond the terror before him.

Keil and Delitzsch are careful why the money is set down so exactly. It is brought forward not merely as a detail of the plot but as the chief and telling point of the whole report — the naked sum at which Haman had valued the extinction of a nation, the bribe by which he had bought the king's leave to destroy them. To lay that figure before the queen was to show her at once the coldness and the completeness of the design: her people had been sold, by weight of silver, into the king's own treasury. The witnesses do not contend. Gill and Keil establish the hard facts — the enmity, the bribe, the plot — while Henry sets those very facts within a heart that has not yet given the cause up for lost, so that the same message which measures the danger also carries, in Mordecai's charge to intercede, the first stirring of the hope that will answer it.
8:
To the spoken report Mordecai adds a document, and the witnesses weigh both the paper and the charge that went with it. The reformed John Gill notes that he gave Hatach a copy of the writing of the decree that had been published at Shushan for the Jews' destruction; the edict being now proclaimed in the city, Mordecai had been able to see it and to transcribe it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the double commission that came with it: Mordecai gave the copy of the decree issued in Susa that Hatach might show it to the queen, and charged him further to declare the matter to her and to command her to go in unto the king, to make supplication before him and request for her people.

The puritan Matthew Henry reads the charge as an appeal to every tie that bound her. Mordecai sent her a true copy of the edict that she might see for herself the imminent danger she and her people were in, and charged her, if she had any respect for him or any kindness for the Jewish nation, to appear now on their behalf — to rectify the misinformations by which the king had been imposed upon, and to set the matter in its true light — not doubting that then the king would vacate the decree. The document, in Henry's reading, is put into her hands precisely so that she cannot plead ignorance of what is at stake.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke notes what the Greek text adds to Mordecai's charge and the Hebrew does not. The Septuagint has him press her with a tender remembrance — recall the days of thy low estate, when thou wast nourished by my hand; and now that Haman, next to the king, has procured a decree for our destruction, pray to the Lord, and plead with the king, that we may be delivered from death. But of all this, Clarke observes, there is not a word in the Hebrew, nor in the Syriac, nor in the Vulgate; it is a later expansion, and one whose very content — the open appeal to prayer and to the Lord — supplies just what the Hebrew story so pointedly withholds.

The witnesses agree on the shape of the moment. Mordecai has turned from lament to strategy: he does not leave the queen to trust rumour, but puts the authenticated decree into her hand, so that she must reckon with the danger in its own black letters, and then binds upon her a threefold charge — to go in unto the king, to make supplication, and to make request before him for her people. The document is the proof, the charge is the demand; and between them they leave Esther no room to plead that she did not know, or did not understand, that a whole nation's life had now been laid, uninvited and at the hazard of her own, at the foot of the throne she shared.
9:
The messenger returns, and the burden crosses at last into the palace. The reformed John Gill states it simply: Hatach came and told Esther the words of Mordecai — and in those words, he adds, lay the whole of it, the case of the Jews, the cause of their danger, and what Mordecai would have her do at this critical juncture. Nothing was kept back; the queen was made to know both the peril and the part she was asked to take in averting it. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the narrative straight on: when Hatach brought Esther this information, she at once sent word back to Mordecai by the same hand — her answer, which the next verses will give, being already forming as the fatal report reached her.

The puritan Matthew Henry keeps before us the strange machinery of the whole conference. Since the queen could hold no direct speech with her kinsman, every message had to be carried to and fro by the trusted eunuch; and it is worth marking, Henry would say, how faithfully the servant discharged his trust, bearing the mourner's full account into the presence of the queen. The verse is a hinge, and the witnesses feel its weight though they say little over it. The grief that began with one man at the gate, and spread to a whole people in every province, has now reached the one person set highest and safest of them all; and it reaches her not as distant news but as a summons touching her own life.

What Hatach lays before Esther is no longer a rumour of Mordecai's sackcloth but the copy of a death-decree and a charge to risk everything. The messenger who first went out in mere concern for a mourning man comes back bearing the fate of a nation; and the historian, having brought the report all the way from the street into the royal apartments, pauses on that delivery before letting the queen speak.

It is worth marking how completely the burden has now shifted. At the chapter's opening the grief was Mordecai's, and then the people's; it reached Esther first only as a vague intimation that moved her to send raiment. Now, by Hatach's faithful telling, she holds the whole of it — the plot, the price, the very words of the decree, and Mordecai's demand that she go in and plead. The commentators do not divide over so plain a verse; they simply register that the crisis has found the one who alone stands near enough to the throne to meet it, and that with her hearing of “the words of Mordecai” the deliverance, or the ruin, of her people has been laid squarely at her door. What she will make of that word the next verses will tell; here the writer only lets it land, and lets the reader feel the silence in which a queen weighs a summons that may cost her life.
10:
Esther answers, and even her answer must go by the hand of another. The reformed John Gill marks the necessity in it: again she spake unto Hatach, for there was no other way of corresponding or conversing, the wives of kings being altogether under the watch and care of such attendants. Not even to send a word to her kinsman could the queen do otherwise than through the eunuch; the confinement that will make her coming intercession so perilous shows itself already in the mere carrying of a message. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply note that she gave Hatach a fresh commission to Mordecai, the substance of which the following verse sets out — her account of the inexorable law that stood in the way.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to a small point of the text. The word “Again” with which our version opens the verse has nothing answering to it in the original; it would be better rendered simply “and,” for the statement here runs on continuously from v.9 — the report brought in, and the reply sent back, forming one unbroken movement of the narrative rather than two separated acts.

The verse has little on its face, and the witnesses do not force it; yet its very plainness carries the theme that governs the whole scene. A queen, seated in the palace of the greatest empire of the age, cannot speak to a mourning man in the square below except by relays of an eunuch. Gill will not let that pass unremarked: there was no other way of corresponding, none, for the wives of kings were kept altogether under the watch and care of such attendants, so that even to frame a reply the queen must borrow another man's feet and mouth. The freedom of the meanest Jew in the street to send his own word where he pleased was denied to the woman who wore the crown.

The distance between the throne and the gate, which the story has been measuring from its first verse, is measured here once more in the smallest coin — the second sending of Hatach, back across the same open place, bearing the queen's answer to the man who had laid upon her a nation's hope. And that answer, Keil reminds us, is no mere acknowledgment but the opening of her defence, her account of the inexorable law that stands between her and the king. So the constraint that shows itself in this small mechanical thing — a message that must go by a servant — is the very constraint she is about to plead as the reason she cannot do what Mordecai asks. What that dread law was, the next verse will set out; here the historian only sets the answer moving, and the commentators, marking the confinement and the continuity, let it move.
11:
Now the queen names the wall that stands between her and the king, and the witnesses gather round that deadly Persian law. The reformed John Gill stresses how universally it was known: not the princes and courtiers only, but all the king's servants and the meanest of his subjects throughout the provinces knew it — so notorious was the rule that whoever came to the king unbidden should die. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the Hebrew closely — there is one law for such, one unvarying sentence — and notes that the monuments at Persepolis show the Persian king in every case grasping a long sceptre in his right hand, the very golden sceptre whose extending alone could spare the life of the intruder. And Ellicott sets a contrast against that terror: how forcibly, after reading such a verse, the self-styled king of kings, whose presence even a suppliant approached on pain of death, stands over against the true King of kings, who himself bids men come and fall low before his footstool.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke fills in the manners of the court. The Persian sovereigns affected an almost divine majesty; into the inner court none might come but at the king's own pleasure, not the greatest of his ministers, nor the most favoured of his women, unless summoned. And Esther's difficulty was sharpened by a further circumstance: she had not been called these thirty days, and Clarke suspects that Haman himself had contrived to keep her from the king's presence, the better to alienate his affection from a queen he knew to be against him. The wesleyan John Wesley reads the law as framed to guard both the majesty and the safety of the king's person, and by the craft of the great officers, that few might have access to him; and he hears in Esther's words a real fear, that her not being called for a month gave her just cause to think the king's affections were cooling toward her.

The puritan Matthew Henry judges the whole statute. It was made, he says, not so much in prudence for the king's safety as in pride, that being seldom seen and hardly approached he might be adored as a little god — a foolish law, which made the palace a kind of prison to the king and shut the subject out from any redress of his grievances. It is not so, Henry rejoices, in the court of the King of kings: to the footstool of his throne of grace we may at any time come boldly, and be sure of an answer of peace to the prayer of faith, welcome even into the holiest through the blood of Jesus. The witnesses agree on the peril Esther faces, and turn it, with one accord, into a foil for the free access that the earthly throne so jealously denied.
12:
A single line carries the queen's fear back to the gate, and the witnesses pause over the bare relay. The reformed John Gill notes only that they told Mordecai Esther's words — the messengers she had sent bearing her answer back to him across the square. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the same turn: when what Esther had said was reported to Mordecai, he sent his reply back to her again — the pressing monition of the verses that follow already gathering in response. The puritan Matthew Henry keeps before us the machinery that makes such a verse necessary at all: the divers messages passing to and fro by Hatach's hand were the only commerce possible between the queen shut within and the mourner standing without.

The historian sets down no more than the fact, and the witnesses honour his reticence; yet the fact is a hinge on which much turns. Esther has pleaded the law, and her plea — the peril of unbidden approach, the thirty days of the king's coldness — now travels back across the palace threshold to the man in sackcloth who first laid the burden on her. For a moment the deliverance of a whole people hangs suspended between them: the queen has said, in effect, that what he asks may cost her life, and the eunuch carries that hesitation to the gate and awaits what the barred kinsman will answer.

It is worth marking how the writer works. He does not tell us Mordecai's feeling as the queen's excuse reaches him; he only reports that her words were told, and lets the suspense of the empty pause do its office. Every step of this embassy has been carried by a servant crossing an open place — the report out, the law back, and now the law delivered — and the reader, following the messenger, is made to wait with Mordecai for a reply that must either accept the queen's fear as final or press her past it.

Keil marks that the answer was not long in coming: as soon as Esther's words were reported, Mordecai returned his pressing monition, the sharp word of the next verse. And there is a quiet irony the commentators leave the reader to catch. The message the eunuch now carries is a queen's plea of helplessness — the deadly law, the thirty days of the king's coldness — laid before a man who has no power at all, who cannot even enter the gate. The one with every earthly advantage confesses she can do nothing; the one with none is about to tell her she must do everything. The commentators add little to so bare a verse, because there is little on the surface to add; but they feel, and make us feel, that the whole cause of Israel hangs for a moment in the silence between one message and the next.
13:
Mordecai's reply comes back hard and unsparing, and the witnesses weigh its edge. The reformed John Gill notes simply that Mordecai commanded an answer to be returned to Esther, charging the messengers what they should carry back from him. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the thrust of it: think not, he warns her, that thou shalt escape in the king's house more than all the Jews — she must not imagine that her place in the palace would save her alone, when the sentence had gone out against her whole people.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke hears in the very warning a further confirmation of what he has suspected all along, that Haman knew something of the kinship between Mordecai and Esther; for Mordecai tells her plainly that within the king's palace she would no more escape than the rest of the Jews without — a danger that presupposes her descent could be discovered and used against her. The threat is not idle: the queen is a Jewess, and the decree that dooms her nation makes no exception for the crown.

The puritan Matthew Henry draws out the reasoning by which Mordecai presses her. It was, first of all, her own cause, for the decree to destroy all the Jews did not except her: think not therefore, he in effect says, that the palace will be thy protection and the crown save thy head; thou art a Jewess, and if the rest be cut off, thou wilt be cut off too. It was certainly her wisdom, Henry adds, rather to expose herself to a conditional death from her husband — a death only possible, and that at the king's displeasure — than to wait in her chamber for a death made certain by her enemy's edict. The one danger she might yet avert; the other, if she kept silent, would surely find her out.

The witnesses do not divide over the verse; together they show Mordecai stripping away the one refuge Esther might have supposed she had. Her royalty is no sanctuary; the wall of the harem that keeps her from the king will not keep out Haman's edict, and the very concealment of her descent, which had raised her, might now be pierced to her ruin. If she thinks to be silent and safe, Mordecai answers, she has mistaken both her danger and her duty. And the argument is not cruelty but kindness: he will not flatter her into a false security that would prove her grave. The next verse will press that answer to its height, opening beyond the bare threat a larger providence in which her very throne was given her for this hour.
14:
Here the messages reach their climax, and the witnesses divide over the faith that speaks in them. The reformed John Gill sets the case: if Esther should altogether hold her peace at this time, keeping silence for fear of the danger, refusing to speak to the king for her people. Against that silence Mordecai lays a double certainty. The puritan Matthew Henry hears in the first of them the accent of a strong faith: enlargement and deliverance would arise to the Jews from another place, though she failed them — a confidence that staggered not at the promise when the danger was most threatening, but against hope believed in hope, for instruments may fail, yet God's covenant will not. And the second certainty is a warning to herself: if she deserted her friends now through cowardice, she and her father's house would be destroyed while the rest of the Jews were preserved; he that by sinful shifts will save his life shall lose it. Above all, Henry says, divine Providence had an eye to this in raising her to the throne — who knows whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this? — so that she was bound in gratitude to answer the very end of her elevation.

The wesleyan voices press the same providence. John Wesley reads “from another place” as the language of strong faith, against hope believing in hope, and thinks it probable that God had raised Esther to her honour for this very season. Adam Clarke is equally sure that Mordecai looked for deliverance to come by some means, and judged Esther the likeliest instrument: was she lifted from obscurity, he asks, merely for her own sake, or set where she might counteract one of the most ruinous purposes ever framed? He draws the parallel of the poor wise man who by his wisdom delivered a little city, though afterward no man remembered him, in Eccl. 9:14.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the words with equal care but reads the heart behind them more coldly. “Enlargement” is literally a breathing-space; and “from another place” he takes, with what he calls Mordecai's studied reserve, to mean divine help — yet he doubts it proves any earnestness of faith, for had Mordecai's faith been like that of his more devout countrymen he would have been in Judaea and not in Persia at all. The whole conversation, Ellicott feels, lacks any higher feeling, any suggestion of turning to God; and “thou and thy father's house shall be destroyed” he reads as destruction by the hand of God, who, having raised Esther to this height, will require the duty of her. So the witnesses agree upon the sense and part over the spirit: Henry, Wesley, and Clarke hear in Mordecai a bold and believing trust that God will save his people with her or without her, while Ellicott hears a man reasoning shrewdly from providence, and finds in the exchange a strange absence of the God on whom it silently leans.
15:
The queen's answer turns the whole embassy, and the witnesses mark the moment of her yielding. The reformed John Gill records it plainly: then Esther bade the messengers return this answer to Mordecai, the resolution which the next verse will set out. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse as the fruit of Mordecai's pressing monition — that urgent word had done its work, and Esther now sent back her reply, no longer pleading the law but rising to meet it.

The puritan Matthew Henry dwells on the change that has come over her. Esther hereupon resolved, whatever it might cost her, to make her application to the king; but she would not do it, he observes, until she and her friends had first made their application to God. Let them first, by fasting and prayer, obtain the favour of God, and then she should hope to find favour with the king. The order is everything to Henry: the queen does not fling herself upon the throne in mere desperation, but turns first, and turns others with her, to the God in whose hands the hearts of kings are held, and on whom she now depends to incline this king's heart toward her. And Henry looks ahead with confidence to the outcome: in the sequel of the story, he says, we shall find that God did not say to this seed of Jacob, Seek ye me in vain.

The verse is brief, but it is the pivot of the whole story, and the witnesses feel its force. She who had answered Mordecai's charge with the law's plain sentence of death now answers his second word with consent; the sceptre that might not be approached will be approached after all. And the great reversal that runs to the book's end begins in this single sentence of reply: the intended victim steps forward to become the deliverer, and the first thing she asks for is not a weapon or a stratagem but a fast. Gill notes only that she returned her answer; Keil marks that the pressing admonition prevailed; Henry catches the piety that shapes the reply. But all three see that with Esther's “this answer” the queen has crossed from self-preservation to self-offering, having solemnly commended her cause to God before she ventures it upon a man, so that the deliverance of her people has found at last its willing hand.
16:
Esther's resolution comes at last, and with it the sharpest disagreement of the chapter over the God who is never named. The reformed John Gill takes the first clause soberly: gather all the Jews present in Shushan, she bids Mordecai, that they may be acquainted with her purpose; and he sets aside the later Targum's tale of twelve thousand chosen priests found in the city as a plain exaggeration, since there can hardly have been so many Jews in all Shushan. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read her charge as a call to earnest humiliation: she resolves to go in unto the king unsummoned, but first begs Mordecai and all the Jews to join her and her maidens in a three days' fast, that God's gracious help may be sought before the venture; and though the words “God” and “prayer” are not so much as named, the fast is plainly such a seeking.

The wesleyan Adam Clarke will not let that silence pass. What a strange thing, he exclaims, that still we hear nothing of prayer, nor of God! Yet he cannot believe the queen thought there was any charm in fasting and sackcloth for their own sake: if these humiliations were not meant to turn away the displeasure of God, what were they done for? She must, he concludes, have depended much upon their efficacy. And of her closing words — if I perish, I perish — he says that if she must lose her life in the attempt to save her people, she was resolved to lose it cheerfully. John Wesley reads the command frankly as fasting joined with prayer: leave off your common meals, and give yourselves to constant and fervent supplication; and he takes her maidens to have been either Jewesses or proselytes who fasted with her.

The puritan Matthew Henry gathers the whole into a portrait of faith. Esther spoke as an Israelite, with her eye up to God in whose hand the hearts of kings are; she believed his favour was to be obtained by prayer, that his people are a praying people and he a prayer-hearing God, and she joined fasting with prayer as good people do in extraordinary cases — a mistress praying with her maids. And she spoke as a queen, in a holy resolution: if I perish, I perish; reasoning, as the lepers at the gate in 2 Kings 7:4, that if she sat still she must die, but if she ventured she might live and be the life of her people. So the witnesses part over the book's great reticence: Clarke and the grammatical-historical reading feel the absence of any named God as a thing to be wondered at; Henry, Wesley, and Keil hear, in the fast Esther commands, an unmistakable turning to the God whom the story leaves unnamed but not unsought.
17:
The chapter closes as it opened, with Mordecai in motion, but the direction of his going has been reversed. The reformed John Gill notes that Mordecai went his way to do the business he was now directed to; and he passes on a rabbinic reading of the verb. Jarchi, taking the word in the sense of passing over or transgressing, understood that Mordecai transgressed the festival by this fast: the letter, he reasons, had been written on the thirteenth of Nisan, and the next day was the passover, so that the three fast-days — the fourteenth, fifteenth, and sixteenth — fell within the feast of the passover and of unleavened bread, and were kept in mourning rather than in the appointed joy. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it more plainly: Mordecai went his way from the open place before the court, and did according to all that Esther had commanded him.

The wesleyan John Wesley attends to the reckoning of the three days and nights. They need not be counted to the full, he observes, for Esther went in to the king on the third day; the fast began in the evening, and, since a part of a day is reputed a whole day in the account of Scripture, as at Matt. 12:40, she might keep the fast through two whole nights and a day and the better part of a third and yet go to the king while it lasted.

Brief as it is, the verse quietly completes a reversal the chapter has been working toward. Mordecai had charged the queen, pressed her, all but commanded her; now it is written that Mordecai did according to all that Esther had commanded him. The elder kinsman obeys the young sovereign; the man who could not so much as pass the king's gate goes out to gather a fasting people whose lives will hang upon her venture. There is a fitness in it that the witnesses do not labour but plainly feel: she who was reared by his care now directs his steps, and the guardian becomes the servant of the ward he saved.

The witnesses do not divide over so plain a sentence. Keil marks the ready obedience, Gill the disputed festival and the rabbinic scruple over a fast kept through the passover, Wesley the careful counting of the days; but each leaves Mordecai bending to the will of the queen he had roused. So the chapter that opened with one man's solitary cry in the streets closes with a whole people summoned to a common fast, the embassy of eunuchs and open squares resolved at last into the united humiliation of the Jews of Shushan — all of them now waiting, with the queen, upon the God whom the story will not name, for the one of their number who is about to dare the throne.
